stories.title: The Solution
stories.description: Amit reads Bertolt Brecht's poem 'The Solution', written after the 1953 uprising in East Germany. The poem satirically suggests that if the people have lost the confidence of the government, the government should simply dissolve the people and elect another.

stories.title: Ajay's Mistake at 21
stories.description: Ajay shares a personal regret. At age 21, the economist Kirit Parikh offered him an apprenticeship. Ajay, lured by the 'glamour' of a US PhD and credentialism, turned it down. He now views this as the 'dumbest decision imaginable' and believes the apprenticeship would have been a far superior education.

stories.title: Einstein Riding a Beam of Light
stories.description: Ajay tells the story of Einstein at age 16, who started thinking about what the world would look like if he were riding a beam of light. He stayed with this single problem for years until he arrived at Special Relativity. This illustrates the power of staying with a problem longer than others.

stories.title: The Satellite Imagery Revolution
stories.description: Ajay discusses how satellites taking photos at 1:30 AM can measure prosperity through nighttime lights (pixel size 0.5km x 0.5km). This data allows for independent measurement of economic activity, bypassing potentially unreliable government statistics.

stories.title: The 20-Year Battle for Free Trade
stories.description: Ajay recounts how the 1991 economic reforms in India, specifically the removal of trade barriers, were not a sudden decision but the result of 20 years of intellectual groundwork laid by economists like Bhagwati and Srinivasan, who won the debate against protectionists long before the policy was implemented.

core_ideas.description: Ajay outlines a 'pipeline' for state change: Data -> Research -> Imaginative Solutions -> Public Debate -> Government Committees -> Decisions/Laws -> Implementation. You cannot skip steps; attempting to do so leads to failure.
A fundamental distinction: The State is not the People. Often the State oppresses the People. Real change and creativity come from the People (society), not the State.

Ajay argues against the 'millennial sense' that progress is inevitable. The 20th century (wars, totalitarianism) and recent democratic backsliding show that things can go backwards. 'Political and social catastrophe is always possible.'

Contrasting with the standard view of progress, Ajay argues that the shift from hunter-gatherer to agricultural society was a decline in quality of life (disease, oppression, state control, loss of freedom for women).

Ajay's theory of change: We don't change minds by 100% in a debate. In a 'zone of truth and trust', we might shift our views by 10% over time. If we persuade 10 people by 10%, that is significant social change.

For those wanting to make a change, the most important quality is endurance—the ability to keep going without being transactional or expecting immediate rewards. 'Don't ask for a reward, don't ask for success.'
To sustain the long fight for change, one needs a community of trusted friends ('fellow travelers') who can critique honest failures and support each other.
